title: Risk reduction from an intervention, year by year

blocks.text: 7.3.4 Risk Reduction From an Intervention, Year by Year

GridCap's planners want a second plan next to the NPV plan of lesson 6.4.2: the plan that removes the most failure risk within the same budgets and rules. The start-year model of lesson 6.4.1 can find it, if each variable $`x_{i,s}`$ (project $`i`$ starts in year $`s`$) gets the right objective coefficient: how much risk the project removes if it starts in $`s`$. Lesson 1.1.2 gave each project one number, the risk avoided next year. That cannot tell 2028 from 2030. This lesson builds the coefficient year by year from lessons 7.3.1 to 7.3.3, then solves the plan, in five rules.

GridCap is a fictional utility generated for this course; its assets, projects and budgets describe no real company. Every ID in this lesson is the small portfolio's (tiny and medium reuse the same IDs for other assets).
Work Resets the Asset's Age in the Year After It Ends

Every quantity in this lesson follows from one table: the asset's age in each year, with and without the project. Let $`y_0`$ be the plan's first year (2027), $`a`$ the asset's age in $`y_0`$, $`d`$ the project's years of work and $`\rho`$ the share of its age the asset keeps after the work, lesson 1.1.2's convention: 0 for a replacement, a rebuild or undergrounding, 0.5 for a repair, a trim, a clearing or a widening. Lesson 7.4.1 writes the same reset as a depth $`d = 1 - \rho`$, gives clearing and widening a deeper one, and starts the benefit at the start year; its section *Two Renewal Conventions, One Failure Model* compares the two and says which the course uses where.

items: **Without the project** the asset ages one year per year: $`a^0_y = a + (y - y_0)`$.

**With the project started in $`s`$**, the asset keeps aging during the work, the years $`s, \dots, s + d - 1`$. From year $`s + d`$, the first full year after the work, it is $`\rho`$ times the age it had reached, and it ages one year per year from there:

blocks.text: a^{s}_y = \begin{cases} a + (y - y_0) & y < s + d \\ \rho\,\big(a + (s + d - y_0)\big) + (y - s - d) & y \ge s + d \end{cases}
Small's P024 undergrounds the feeder A024, two years of work, and may start in 2028, 2029 or 2030. Its asset's ages over ten years, for each start:

P024 underground A024 (feeder): age 50 in 2027, beta 2.49, eta 43.1, CoF $3,385k, 2 years of work, keeps 0% of its age
start | asset age by year, 2027-2036
 2028 |   50   51   52    0    1    2    3    4    5    6
 2029 |   50   51   52   53    0    1    2    3    4    5
 2030 |   50   51   52   53   54    0    1    2    3    4

The convention that benefit starts in the year after the work ends is a choice, and a cautious one: a crew may finish in March. Whatever your utility's rule, write it into this one function, so every coefficient follows it.
The Risk Removed in a Year Is the Risk Without the Work Minus the Risk With It
With the two ages, the risk removed in year $`y`$ by a start in $`s`$ is the difference of two yearly risks, each the CoF times the expected failures of lesson 7.3.3:
\delta_{i,s,y} = \text{CoF}\,\Big( \big[\Lambda(a^0_y + 1) - \Lambda(a^0_y)\big] - \big[\Lambda(a^s_y + 1) - \Lambda(a^s_y)\big] \Big)
For P024:

Read it row by row. Nothing is removed before the work ends. After it, the yearly reduction *grows*: the feeder that was not undergrounded keeps wearing out faster than the new cable does. A later start removes a little more in each year it is in service (285 against 270 in its first year), because it takes away an older, riskier asset, but it is in service for fewer years. Over ten years the 2028 start removes $2,013k and the 2030 start $1,487k.
<!-- practice 1 -->
After the Work, the Asset Ages Again

A common shortcut, found in interview notes, writes the reduction as the PoF without the work minus a fixed "post-renewal" PoF, $`(\text{PoF}_{i,y} - \text{PoF}^0) \times C_i`$, as if the renewed asset stayed as good as on the day the crew left. It does not; it starts a new life on the same curve (or on a new design's curve). The program compares the aging version with the frozen one for a replacement and for a repair:

P024 underground started 2028; age after the work, by year: 0 1 2 3 4 5 6
  ten-year reduction: asset ages again $2,013k, frozen after the work $2,048k, overstated by 2%
P027 repair started 2029; age after the work, by year: 21 22 23 24 25 26
  ten-year reduction: asset ages again $2,451k, frozen after the work $2,638k, overstated by 8%

For a replacement the error is small over ten years, because a new asset's hazard is tiny for its first years. For a repair it is four times larger: the repaired transformer restarts at 21 years old, where its hazard is already climbing, and freezing it there ignores that climb. The longer the counting window, the larger the error. The cost of doing it right is nothing: the yearly computation is one function either way.
Count the Reduction Over a Fixed Window and Discount It
Two decisions turn the yearly reductions into one coefficient.

**Which years count.** Counting only the plan's own years (2027 to 2031 for GridCap small) gives the "plan years" column above: $546k, $277k and 0 for P024's three starts. A start in 2030 finishes in 2031 and removes no risk inside the plan, so the model would never start it late, and would favor short projects over long ones for the same reason. This is the **end-of-horizon effect**. The fix is to count every start over the same **evaluation window** $`W`$, long enough to include each project's service after the plan ends. This course uses ten years from the plan's first year, 2027 to 2036, the "ten years" column.

**How to weigh later years.** A dollar of failure cost avoided in 2036 is worth less today than one avoided in 2028, for the reason lesson 7.2.1 (*Financial evaluation*) gives for cash flows. Discount each year at the portfolio's rate $`r`$ (7% for GridCap) back to $`y_0`$:
\text{rr}_{i,s} = \sum_{y \in W} \frac{\delta_{i,s,y}}{(1 + r)^{\,y - y_0}}
Here `years` is the evaluation window, not the plan's years. Six projects' coefficients:

Every coefficient falls with a later start: each year of delay is a year the old asset's risk is carried. P001 and P002 are the replacement and the repair of the same line A001: the one-year repair starting in 2027 removes more over the window than the two-year replacement starting in 2028, because it is in service two years sooner. Those two projects form an alternative group, and the model, not a ranking, decides between them.
<!-- practice 2 -->
The Coefficients Enter the Start-Year Model Unchanged
The model is lesson 6.4.2's, whole, with only the objective's coefficients replaced: $`\text{rr}_{i,t}`$ where lesson 6.4.2 had $`\text{npv}_{i,t}`$.

**Sets.** $`P`$ the projects; $`Y`$ the plan's years; $`T_i \subseteq Y`$ the start years project $`i`$ may use; $`M \subseteq P`$ the must-do projects; $`\mathcal{G}`$ the alternative groups; $`C \subseteq P`$ the child projects, with parent $`p(c)`$ and lag $`L_c`$ years; $`W`$ the evaluation window, ten years from $`y_0`$.

**Parameters.** $`\text{rr}_{i,t}`$, the discounted risk removed over $`W`$ if project $`i`$ starts in year $`t`$ ($k, the formula of the previous section); $`c_{i,k}`$, what project $`i`$ spends in its $`k`$-th year of work ($k); $`B_y`$, the budget of year $`y`$ ($k).
**Variables.** $`x_{i,t} \in \{0, 1\}`$ for every $`i \in P`$ and $`t \in T_i`$: project $`i`$ starts in year $`t`$.
**Objective.**
\max \; \sum_{i \in P} \sum_{t \in T_i} \text{rr}_{i,t}\, x_{i,t} \quad \leftarrow \text{this lesson}
**Constraints.**

\begin{aligned}
\sum_{t \in T_i} x_{i,t} &\le 1 && \forall i \in P \setminus M && \text{(once}_i) \\
\sum_{t \in T_i} x_{i,t} &= 1 && \forall i \in M && \text{(must}_i) \\
\sum_{i \in g} \sum_{t \in T_i} x_{i,t} &\le 1 && \forall g \in \mathcal{G} && \text{(alt}_g) \\
\sum_{u \in T_c,\, u \le t} x_{c,u} &\le \sum_{s \in T_{p(c)},\, s \le t - L_c} x_{p(c),s} && \forall c \in C,\ t \in T_c && \text{(after}_{c,t}) \\
\sum_{i \in P} \sum_{t \in T_i,\, t \le y} c_{i,\,y-t}\, x_{i,t} &\le B_y && \forall y \in Y && \text{(budget}_y)
\end{aligned}

The builder takes the coefficients as a dict keyed by `(project, start year)`, so the same function builds the NPV model and the risk model. It is written with MathOpt, the OR-Tools modeling layer of section 4: binary variables with `add_binary_variable`, rows with `add_linear_constraint`, and the objective with `maximize`, solved by HiGHS:
model.maximize(sum(coefficient[key] * var for key, var in x.items()))

for name, objective in (("max NPV", npv), ("max risk reduction", rr)):
    sm = build(small, objective)
    result = solve_highs(sm.model)
    plans[name] = plan = plan_of(sm, result)
    print(f"{name:18}: {len(plan)} projects, NPV ${sum(npv[k] for k in plan.items()):,}k, "
          f"risk removed ${sum(rr[k] for k in plan.items()):,.0f}k ({result.termination.reason.name})")

max NPV           : 27 projects, NPV $24,260k, risk removed $10,577k (OPTIMAL)
max risk reduction: 31 projects, NPV $18,886k, risk removed $16,086k (OPTIMAL)
projects in both plans: 21

The NPV plan is the one lesson 6.4.1 found ($24,260k), which lesson 6.4.2's spread-cost model finds again. The risk plan removes $16,086k of discounted failure cost against the NPV plan's $10,577k, 52% more, and gives up $5,374k of NPV to do it. The plans share 21 projects. Neither is "the" plan; they are two ends of a trade-off, and section 8 builds the plans between them.

The model leaves out one family of rows: the region floors $`\text{floor}_r`$ of lesson 7.1.3, which the floored base scenario of that lesson includes. Dropping rows can only let a plan do better, and here neither plan does: both already fund more than every floor, so each is feasible with the floors in, and a plan that is optimal without some rows and keeps them is optimal with them. The program checks each plan's capex by region against the floors:

max NPV: capex funded above each region floor ($k): Ridge 5,860, Valley 8,430, Coast 9,680, Plains 3,710; every floor met: True
max risk reduction: capex funded above each region floor ($k): Ridge 7,480, Valley 5,180, Coast 7,530, Plains 6,000; every floor met: True

That is why the NPV plan here has the same $24,260k as lesson 7.1.3's base scenario, floors and all: the floors do not bind on this data. On a portfolio where one did, the row $`\sum_{i \in P_r} \text{capex}_i \sum_{t \in T_i} x_{i,t} \ge F_r`$ goes back in unchanged.
**The RUL question of lesson 7.3.2, answered.** Rebuild every asset's curve with the scale that makes its GridCap RUL the median remaining life, recompute the coefficients and solve again:
with eta calibrated to each RUL: 30 projects, risk removed by the curve's own measure $15,999k; projects that differ: P013, P014, P020

Three projects change, and measured by the original curves the RUL-based plan removes $87k less, about 0.5%, although ten assets with an RUL at the floor of 1 (lesson 7.3.2) now carry a PoF of 50% a year. On this data the plan barely depends on which source of curves is used. That is a finding about this data, not a rule: on another portfolio the same disagreement could move many projects, and the way to know is to solve both, as here.
<!-- practice 3 -->
Summary

items: **Work resets the asset's age in the year after it ends.** Before that the asset keeps aging; after it, it is $`\rho`$ times the age it had reached and ages again.
**The risk removed in a year is the risk without the work minus the risk with it.** Each is CoF times the expected failures of that year's age.
**After the work, the asset ages again.** Freezing the post-work risk overstated a repair's ten-year reduction by 8% on GridCap small.
**Count the reduction over a fixed window and discount it.** Counting only the plan's years gives late starts zero; a ten-year window from $`y_0`$, discounted at 7%, gives $`\text{rr}_{i,s}`$.
**The coefficients enter the start-year model unchanged.** On GridCap small the risk plan removes 52% more risk than the NPV plan and gives up $5,374k of NPV.

blocks.text: **Further reading:** [OR-Tools, MathOpt basic example](https://developers.google.com/optimization/math_opt/basic_example) (building a MathOpt model, `maximize`, solving and reading the termination reason and objective value, the calls the risk model uses); [NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook, the NHPP power law model](https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/apr/section1/apr172.htm) (expected failures of a repairable system growing as a power of age, the count each yearly risk is built on); [NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook, the Weibull distribution](https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/apr/section1/apr162.htm) (the cumulative hazard $`(t/\eta)^\beta`$); [SciPy, `scipy.stats.weibull_min`](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.weibull_min.html) (`logsf`, used by the practices to check every coefficient).
Challenges

items: Count P024's reduction over a 15-year window instead of 10. Predict whether the gap between its 2028 and 2030 coefficients grows or shrinks.
A replacement installs a new design with shape 2.0 and scale 70 years instead of the old curve. Which line of `yearly_reduction` changes?
Some utilities count the risk removed only until the asset's next planned renewal, say 40 years for a pole. What does that do to the coefficients of a replacement compared with a repair?

blocks.text: Design Note: Why the Coefficient Is Precomputed

The risk of an asset in a year is a nonlinear function of its age, and the age depends on the decision. Writing that inside the model would need nonlinear constraints or piecewise curves (lessons 6.6.1 to 6.6.4). It is not needed here: each start year fixes the whole age path, so every consequence of choosing $`x_{i,s} = 1`$ can be computed before the solve, and the model stays a linear one in binary variables. The price is one coefficient per project and start year, which the model already has a variable for. The same trick works for anything that depends only on *which* start is chosen: NPV (lesson 7.2.4), risk, emissions. It stops working when the value of one project depends on another's choice, such as two projects on the same feeder: then the pair needs a variable or a row of its own, as the bundles and alternatives of lessons 6.5.2 and 6.5.3 do.
The Full Programs

Each snippet above is part of a complete program, and each program printed the output the lesson shows. Open one to read it whole, change it, and run it again: Run starts the program on your copy of the code, so the course's own files never change.

**yearly_reduction.py.** Prints P024's asset ages and its yearly risk reduction for each start year, over the plan and over ten years (*Work Resets the Asset's Age*, *The Risk Removed in a Year*). *Try:* Switch to P027, a repair. Predict whether its yearly reductions grow or shrink after the work.

**constant_vs_aging.py.** Compares the year-by-year reduction with a frozen post-work risk for a replacement and a repair (*After the Work, the Asset Ages Again*). *Try:* Extend `window` to 2046. Predict the new overstatement for P027.

**rr_coefficients.py.** Prints six projects' coefficients by start year, discounted and not (*Count the Reduction Over a Fixed Window*). *Try:* Set `WINDOW` to 5 in `risk_model.py`. Predict which coefficients become 0.

**risk_plan.py.** Solves GridCap small for the most NPV and for the most risk removed, then again with RUL-calibrated curves (*The Coefficients Enter the Start-Year Model Unchanged*). *Try:* Use the undiscounted coefficients (`rate=0.0`). Predict whether the risk plan starts more projects early.
**risk_model.py.** The start-year model builder and `risk_coefficients`.
**asset_curves.py.** The module's library, with `ages_by_year`, `yearly_reduction` and `risk_reduction`.
